# pallet_staking_async - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pallet-staking-async/0.14.0/pallet_staking_async/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#staking-async-pallet)Staking Async Pallet

This pallet is a fork of the original `pallet-staking`, with a number of key differences:

- It no longer has access to a secure timestamp, previously used to calculate the duration of an era.
- It no longer has access to a pallet-session.
- It no longer has access to a pallet-authorship.
- It is capable of working with a multi-page `ElectionProvider``, aka.`pallet-election-provider-multi-block`.

While `pallet-staking` was somewhat general-purpose, this pallet is absolutely NOT right from
the get-go: It is designed to be used ONLY in Polkadot/Kusama AssetHub system parachains.

[§](https://docs.rs#reward-and-inflation)Reward and Inflation

This pallet supports two reward modes, controlled by [ Config::DisableMinting](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.DisableMinting):

[§](https://docs.rs#non-minting-mode-disableminting--true)Non-minting mode (`DisableMinting = true`)

Staking does **not** mint tokens. It expects an external source (e.g. `pallet-dap`) to
fund the general staker reward pot ([ PotAccountProvider](https://docs.rs/trait.PotAccountProvider.html)). At each era boundary,
staking snapshots the accumulated balance into an era-specific pot via

[. Payouts transfer from the era pot.](https://docs.rs/reward/struct.EraRewardManager.html)

`EraRewardManager`Unclaimed rewards from expired eras (past `HistoryDepth`) are withdrawn and passed to
[ Config::UnclaimedRewardHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.UnclaimedRewardHandler).

[ DisableMintingGuard](https://docs.rs/type.DisableMintingGuard.html) is set on the first successful snapshot as a safety net — it
prevents the payout side from falling back to legacy minting for eras that should have
reward pots.

[§](https://docs.rs#legacy-minting-mode-disableminting--false)Legacy minting mode (`DisableMinting = false`)

At era boundary, [ Config::EraPayout](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.EraPayout) computes inflation based on

`total_staked`,
`total_issuance`, and era duration. Tokens are minted on-the-fly during `payout_stakers`.
The treasury remainder is sent to [.](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.RewardRemainder)

`Config::RewardRemainder`[can cap the staker portion.](https://docs.rs/type.MaxStakedRewards.html)

`MaxStakedRewards`[caps the effective era duration.](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.MaxEraDuration)

`Config::MaxEraDuration`This mode is kept for Kusama/non-polkadot runtime’s compatibility where inflation depends on the staking ratio.

[§](https://docs.rs#switching-modes)Switching modes

Switching from legacy to non-minting is a one-way migration. Once `DisableMinting` is
set to `true`, it must **never** be switched back — eras created in non-minting mode
have funded reward pots, and switching to legacy would orphan those pots and cause
double-minting.

[§](https://docs.rs#slashing-pipeline-and-withdrawal-restrictions)Slashing Pipeline and Withdrawal Restrictions

This pallet implements a robust slashing mechanism that ensures the integrity of the staking system while preventing stakers from withdrawing funds that might still be subject to slashing.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview-of-the-slashing-pipeline)Overview of the Slashing Pipeline

The slashing process consists of multiple phases:

- **Offence Reporting**: Offences are reported from the relay chain through- `on_new_offences`
- **Queuing**: Valid offences are added to the- `OffenceQueue`for processing
- **Processing**: Offences are processed incrementally over multiple blocks
- **Application**: Slashes are either applied immediately or deferred based on configuration

[§](https://docs.rs#phase-1-offence-reporting)Phase 1: Offence Reporting

Offences are reported from the relay chain (e.g., from BABE, GRANDPA, BEEFY, or parachain
modules) through the `on_new_offences` function:

```
struct Offence {
    offender: AccountId,        // The validator being slashed
    reporters: Vec<AccountId>,  // Who reported the offence (may be empty)
    slash_fraction: Perbill,    // Percentage of stake to slash
}
```
**Reporting Deadlines**:

- With deferred slashing: Offences must be reported within `SlashDeferDuration - 1`eras
- With immediate slashing: Offences can be reported up to `BondingDuration`eras old

Example: If `SlashDeferDuration = 27` and current era is 100:

- Oldest reportable offence: Era 74 (100 - 26)
- Offences from era 73 or earlier are rejected

[§](https://docs.rs#phase-2-queuing)Phase 2: Queuing

When an offence passes validation, it’s added to the queue:

- **Storage**: Added to- `OffenceQueue`:- `(EraIndex, AccountId) -> OffenceRecord`
- **Era Tracking**: Era added to- `OffenceQueueEras`(sorted vector of eras with offences)
- **Duplicate Handling**: If an offence already exists for the same validator in the same era, only the higher slash fraction is kept

[§](https://docs.rs#phase-3-processing)Phase 3: Processing

Offences are processed incrementally in `on_initialize` each block:

```
1. Load oldest offence from queue
2. Move to `ProcessingOffence` storage
3. For each exposure page (from last to first):
   - Calculate slash for validator's own stake
   - Calculate slash for each nominator (pro-rata based on exposure)
   - Track total slash and reward amounts
4. Once all pages processed, create `UnappliedSlash`
```
**Key Features**:

- **Page-by-page processing**: Large validator sets don’t overwhelm a single block
- **Pro-rata slashing**: Nominators slashed proportionally to their stake
- **Reward calculation**: A portion goes to reporters (if any)

[§](https://docs.rs#phase-4-application)Phase 4: Application

Based on `SlashDeferDuration`, slashes are either:

**Immediate (SlashDeferDuration = 0)**:

- Applied right away in the same block
- Funds deducted from staking ledger immediately

**Deferred (SlashDeferDuration > 0)**:

- Stored in `UnappliedSlashes`for future application
- Applied at era: `offence_era + SlashDeferDuration`
- Can be cancelled by governance before application

[§](https://docs.rs#storage-items-involved)Storage Items Involved

- `OffenceQueue`: Pending offences to process
- `OffenceQueueEras`: Sorted list of eras with offences
- `ProcessingOffence`: Currently processing offence
- `ValidatorSlashInEra`: Tracks highest slash per validator per era
- `UnappliedSlashes`: Deferred slashes waiting for application

[§](https://docs.rs#withdrawal-restrictions)Withdrawal Restrictions

To maintain slashing guarantees, withdrawals are restricted:

**Withdrawal Era Calculation**:

```
earliest_era_to_withdraw = min(
    active_era,
    last_fully_processed_offence_era + BondingDuration
)
```
**Example**:

- Active era: 100
- Oldest unprocessed offence: Era 70
- BondingDuration: 28
- Withdrawal allowed only for chunks with era ≤ 97 (70 - 1 + 28)

**Withdrawal Timeline Example with an Offence**:

```
Era:        90    91    92    93    94    95    96    97    98    99    100   ...  117   118
            |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |          |     |
Unbond:     U
Offence:    X
Reported:               R
Processed:              P (within next few blocks)
Slash Applied:                                                                       S
Withdraw:                                                                            ❌    ✓
With BondingDuration = 28 and SlashDeferDuration = 27:
- User unbonds in era 90
- Offence occurs in era 90
- Reported in era 92 (typically within 2 days, but reportable until Era 116)
- Processed in era 92 (within next few blocks after reporting)
- Slash deferred for 27 eras, applied at era 117 (90 + 27)
- Cannot withdraw unbonded chunks until era 118 (90 + 28)
The 28-era bonding duration ensures that any offences committed before or during
unbonding have time to be reported, processed, and applied before funds can be
withdrawn. This provides a window for governance to cancel slashes that may have
resulted from software bugs.
```
**Key Restrictions**:

- Cannot withdraw if previous era has unapplied slashes
- Cannot withdraw funds from eras with unprocessed offences

- [Eras](https://docs.rs/type.ErasTotalStake.html)- Total - Stake
- The total amount staked for the last `Config::HistoryDepth`
- [Eras](https://docs.rs/type.ErasValidatorIncentiveBudget.html)- Validator - Incentive - Budget
- The total validator incentive budget for the given era, snapshotted at era end.
- [Eras](https://docs.rs/type.ErasValidatorIncentiveWeight.html)- Validator - Incentive - Weight
- Individual validator incentive weight per era.
Each validator’s share of the incentive pot = `their_weight / sum_weight`.
- [Eras](https://docs.rs/type.ErasValidatorPrefs.html)- Validator - Prefs
- Exposure of validator at era with the preferences of validators.
- [Eras](https://docs.rs/type.ErasValidatorReward.html)- Validator - Reward
- The total staker reward budget for each era within `Config::HistoryDepth`
- [Force](https://docs.rs/type.ForceEra.html)- Era
- Mode of era forcing.
- [Hard](https://docs.rs/type.HardCapSelfStake.html)- CapSelf - Stake
- Hard cap on effective validator self-stake.
- [Last](https://docs.rs/type.LastValidatorEra.html)- Validator - Era
- Tracks the last era in which an account was active as a validator (included in the era’s exposure/snapshot).
- [Ledger](https://docs.rs/type.Ledger.html)
- Map from all (unlocked) “controller” accounts to the info regarding the staking.
- [MaxCommission](https://docs.rs/type.MaxCommission.html)
- The maximum commission that validators can set.
- [MaxNominations](https://docs.rs/type.MaxNominationsOf.html)- Of
- Maximum number of nominations per nominator.
- [MaxNominators](https://docs.rs/type.MaxNominatorsCount.html)- Count
- The maximum nominator count before we stop allowing new validators to join.
- [MaxStaked](https://docs.rs/type.MaxStakedRewards.html)- Rewards
- Maximum staked rewards, i.e. the percentage of the era inflation that is used for stake rewards.
- [MaxValidators](https://docs.rs/type.MaxValidatorsCount.html)- Count
- The maximum validator count before we stop allowing new validators to join.
- [MaxWinners](https://docs.rs/type.MaxWinnersOf.html)- Of

- [MaxWinners](https://docs.rs/type.MaxWinnersPerPageOf.html)- PerPage - Of

# tytanic_filter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tytanic-filter/0.4.0/tytanic_filter/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tytanic-filter)`tytanic-filter`

Filtering Tytanic test suites effectively.

This crates provides default implementations for the [ Filter](https://docs.rs/tytanic-core/0.4.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tytanic_core/filter/trait.Filter.html) trait, these
filters are used in the Tytanic CLI.

[§](https://docs.rs#exact-filter-sets)Exact Filter Sets

Exact filter sets can be turned into [ ExactFilter](https://docs.rs/exact/struct.ExactFilter.html), being an exact filter
means they emit errors when expected tests are missing once

[is called.](https://docs.rs/tytanic-core/0.4.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tytanic_core/filter/trait.FilterState.html#method.finish)

`FilterState::finish`[§](https://docs.rs#test-set-expressions)Test Set Expressions

Tests sets are expressions in a set-based DSL for filtering tests according to their identifiers, attributes, and annotations.

Test sets can be parsed and evaluated into an [ ExpressionFilter](https://docs.rs/test_set/struct.ExpressionFilter.html), unlike
explicit filters these are purely additive, i.e. missing tests do not cause
an error.

# cfg_aliases 0.2.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cfg_aliases/0.2.1

# CFG Aliases

CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [`cfg_aliases!`] macro that doesn't have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in `syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.

You use the the [`cfg_aliases!`] macro in your `build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.

## Example

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[]
 = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**

```
use cfg_aliases;
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:

```
println!;
println!;
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
println!;
println!;
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!

```
if cfg!  else
compile_error!;
```
## Syntax and Error Messages

The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.

Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn't a real limitation because that doesn't make logical sense anyway:

```
// This causes an error!
cfg_aliases!
```
## Attribution and Thanks

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3)some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2)the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the `tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`[bringing it up](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13)on the Rust forum.

---

# cfg_aliases - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cfg_aliases/0.2.1/target-redirect/cfg_aliases/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cfg-aliases)CFG Aliases

CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro that doesn’t have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in

`syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.You use the the [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro in your

`build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[build-dependencies]
cfg_aliases = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**

```
use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
fn main() {
    // Setup cfg aliases
    cfg_aliases! {
        // Platforms
        wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
        android: { target_os = "android" },
        macos: { target_os = "macos" },
        linux: { target_os = "linux" },
        // Backends
        surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
        glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
        wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
        dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
    }
}
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:

```
#[cfg(wasm)]
println!("This is running in WASM");
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
println!("We're running in WASM");
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "22")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!

```
if cfg!(glutin) {
    // use glutin
} else {
    // Do something else
}
#[cfg(all(glutin, surfman))]
compile_error!("You cannot specify both `glutin` and `surfman` features");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#syntax-and-error-messages)Syntax and Error Messages

The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.

Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn’t a real limitation because that doesn’t make logical sense anyway:

[§](https://docs.rs#attribution-and-thanks)Attribution and Thanks

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3)some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2)the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the `tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`[bringing it up](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13)on the Rust forum.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html)- aliases
- Create `cfg`aliases

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg_aliases/0.2.1/src/cfg_aliases/lib.rs.html

# cfg_aliases/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # CFG Aliases
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [`cfg_aliases!`] macro that doesn't have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in `syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! You use the the [`cfg_aliases!`] macro in your `build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! ## Example
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! **Cargo.toml:**
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ```toml
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! [build-dependencies]
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! cfg_aliases = "0.1.0"
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! ```
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! **build.rs:**
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ```rust
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! fn main() {
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     // Setup cfg aliases
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!     cfg_aliases! {
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!         // Platforms
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!         wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!         android: { target_os = "android" },
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!         macos: { target_os = "macos" },
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!         linux: { target_os = "linux" },
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!         // Backends
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!         glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!         wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!         dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!     }
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! }
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! ```
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! ```rust
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! #[cfg(wasm)]
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! println!("This is running in WASM");
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! #[cfg(surfman)]
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!     // Do stuff related to surfman
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! }
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! #[cfg(dummy)]
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ```rust
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! #[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! println!("We're running in WASM");
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! #[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "22")))]
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! {
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     // Do stuff related to surfman
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! }
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! #[cfg(not(any(
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     target_arch = "wasm32",
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! )))]
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ```rust
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! if cfg!(glutin) {
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     // use glutin
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! } else {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!     // Do something else
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! }
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! #[cfg(all(glutin, surfman))]
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! compile_error!("You cannot specify both `glutin` and `surfman` features");
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! ## Syntax and Error Messages
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn't a real limitation because that doesn't make logical sense anyway:
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! ```rust,ignore
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! // This causes an error!
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! cfg_aliases! {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!     test1: { not(test2) },
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!     test2: { not(test1) },
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! }
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! ```
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!

[114](https://docs.rs#114)// In the `cfg_aliases!` macro below, all of the rules that start with @parser were derived from
[115](https://docs.rs#115)// the `target_cfg!` macro here:
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//
[117](https://docs.rs#117)// https://docs.rs/tectonic_cfg_support/0.0.1/src/tectonic_cfg_support/lib.rs.html#166-298.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//

[121](https://docs.rs#121)// Also check out this forum topic for more history on the macro development:

[124](https://docs.rs#124)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// Create `cfg` aliases
[126](https://docs.rs#126)///
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// **build.rs:**
[128](https://docs.rs#128)///
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// ```rust
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// # use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// // Setup cfg aliases
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// cfg_aliases! {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///     // Platforms
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///     wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///     android: { target_os = "android" },
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     macos: { target_os = "macos" },
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///     linux: { target_os = "linux" },
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///     // Backends
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///     surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///     glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///     wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///     dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// }
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// ```
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// After you put this in your build script you can then check for those conditions like so:
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// ```rust
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// #[cfg(surfman)]
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)///     // Do stuff related to surfman
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// #[cfg(dummy)]
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:
[159](https://docs.rs#159)///
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// ```rust
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// #[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")))]
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)///     // Do stuff related to surfman
[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// #[cfg(not(any(
[167](https://docs.rs#167)///     target_arch = "wasm32",
[168](https://docs.rs#168)///     all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[169](https://docs.rs#169)///     all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[170](https://docs.rs#170)///     all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
[171](https://docs.rs#171)/// )))]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// ```
[174](https://docs.rs#174)#[macro_export]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)macro_rules! cfg_aliases {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    // Helper that just checks whether the CFG environment variable is set
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    (@cfg_is_set $cfgname:ident) => {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            let cfg_var = stringify!($cfgname).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_");
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            let result = std::env::var(format!("CARGO_CFG_{}", &cfg_var)).is_ok();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            // CARGO_CFG_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS _should_ be set for when debug assertions are enabled,
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            // but as of writing is not: see https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/5777
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            if !result && cfg_var == "DEBUG_ASSERTIONS" {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)                std::env::var("PROFILE") == Ok("debug".to_owned())
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            } else {
[187](https://docs.rs#187)                result
[188](https://docs.rs#188)            }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    };
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    // Helper to check for the presense of a feature
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    (@cfg_has_feature $feature:expr) => {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            std::env::var(
[195](https://docs.rs#195)                format!(
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                    "CARGO_FEATURE_{}",
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                    &stringify!($feature).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_").replace('"', "")
[198](https://docs.rs#198)                )
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            ).map(|x| x == "1").unwrap_or(false)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    };
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    // Helper that checks whether a CFG environment contains the given value
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    (@cfg_contains $cfgname:ident = $cfgvalue:expr) => {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        std::env::var(
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            format!(
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                "CARGO_CFG_{}",
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                &stringify!($cfgname).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_")
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            )
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        ).unwrap_or("".to_owned()).split(",").find(|x| x == &$cfgvalue).is_some()
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    };
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    // Emitting `any(clause1,clause2,...)`: convert to `$crate::cfg_aliases!(clause1) && $crate::cfg_aliases!(clause2) && ...`
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    (
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        @parser_emit
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        all
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    ) => {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        ($(
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            ($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($grouped)+))
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        )&&+)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    };
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    // Likewise for `all(clause1,clause2,...)`.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    (
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        @parser_emit
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        any
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ) => {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        ($(
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            ($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($grouped)+))
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        )||+)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    };
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // "@clause" rules are used to parse the comma-separated lists. They munch
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    // their inputs token-by-token and finally invoke an "@emit" rule when the
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    // list is all grouped. The general pattern for recording the parser state
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    // is:
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    //
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    // ```
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    // $crate::cfg_aliases!(
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    //    @clause $operation
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    //    [{grouped-clause-1} {grouped-clause-2...}]
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    //    [not-yet-parsed-tokens...]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    //    current-clause-tokens...
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    // )
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    // ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    // This rule must come first in this section. It fires when the next token
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    // to parse is a comma. When this happens, we take the tokens in the
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    // current clause and add them to the list of grouped clauses, adding
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    // delimeters so that the grouping can be easily extracted again in the
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    // emission stage.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    (
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        @parser_clause
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        $op:ident
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        [, $($rest:tt)*]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        $($current:tt)+
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ) => {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause $op [
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            $(
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                {$($grouped)+}
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            )*
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            {$($current)+}
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        ] [
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            $($rest)*
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        ]);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    };
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    // This rule comes next. It fires when the next un-parsed token is *not* a
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    // comma. In this case, we add that token to the list of tokens in the
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    // current clause, then move on to the next one.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    (
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        @parser_clause
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        $op:ident
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        [$tok:tt $($rest:tt)*]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        $($current:tt)*
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ) => {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause $op [
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            $(
[283](https://docs.rs#283)                {$($grouped)+}
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            )*
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        ] [
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            $($rest)*
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        ] $($current)* $tok);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    };
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    // This rule fires when there are no more tokens to parse in this list. We
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    // finish off the "current" token group, then delegate to the emission
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    // rule.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    (
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        @parser_clause
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        $op:ident
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        []
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        $($current:tt)+
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ) => {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_emit $op
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            $(
[302](https://docs.rs#302)                {$($grouped)+}
[303](https://docs.rs#303)            )*
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            {$($current)+}
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        );
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    };
[307](https://docs.rs#307)
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    // `all(clause1, clause2...)` : we must parse this comma-separated list and
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    // partner with `@emit all` to output a bunch of && terms.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    (
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        @parser
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        all($($tokens:tt)+)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ) => {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause all [] [$($tokens)+])
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    };
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    // Likewise for `any(clause1, clause2...)`
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    (
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        @parser
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        any($($tokens:tt)+)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    ) => {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause any [] [$($tokens)+])
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    };
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // `not(clause)`: compute the inner clause, then just negate it.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    (
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        @parser
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        not($($tokens:tt)+)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    ) => {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        !($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($tokens)+))
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    };
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    // `feature = value`: test for a feature.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    (@parser feature = $value:expr) => {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_has_feature $value)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    };
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    // `param = value`: test for equality.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    (@parser $key:ident = $value:expr) => {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_contains $key = $value)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    };
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    // Parse a lone identifier that might be an alias
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    (@parser $e:ident) => {
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        __cfg_aliases_matcher__!($e)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    };
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    // Entrypoint that defines the matcher
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    (
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        @with_dollar[$dol:tt]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        $( $alias:ident : { $($config:tt)* } ),* $(,)?
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    ) => {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        // Create a macro that expands other aliases and outputs any non
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        // alias by checking whether that CFG value is set
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        macro_rules! __cfg_aliases_matcher__ {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            // Parse config expression for the alias
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            $(
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                ( $alias ) => {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                    $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($config)*)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                };
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            )*
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            // Anything that doesn't match evaluate the item
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            ( $dol e:ident ) => {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_is_set $dol e)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)            };
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        $(
[368](https://docs.rs#368)            println!("cargo:rustc-check-cfg=cfg({})", stringify!($alias));
[369](https://docs.rs#369)            if $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($config)*) {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)                println!("cargo:rustc-cfg={}", stringify!($alias));
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            }
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        )*
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    };
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    // Catch all that starts the macro
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    ($($tokens:tt)*) => {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@with_dollar[$] $($tokens)*)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    }
[379](https://docs.rs#379)}

# cfg_aliases in cfg_aliases - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg_aliases/0.2.1/cfg_aliases/macro.cfg_aliases.html

```
macro_rules! cfg_aliases {
    (@cfg_is_set $cfgname:ident) => { ... };
    (@cfg_has_feature $feature:expr) => { ... };
    (@cfg_contains $cfgname:ident = $cfgvalue:expr) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_emit
        all
        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_emit
        any
        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        [, $($rest:tt)*]
        $($current:tt)+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        [$tok:tt $($rest:tt)*]
        $($current:tt)*
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        []
        $($current:tt)+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        all($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        any($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        not($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (@parser feature = $value:expr) => { ... };
    (@parser $key:ident = $value:expr) => { ... };
    (@parser $e:ident) => { ... };
    (
        @with_dollar[$dol:tt]
        $( $alias:ident : { $($config:tt)* } ),* $(,)?
    ) => { ... };
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Create `cfg` aliases

**build.rs:**

```
// Setup cfg aliases
cfg_aliases! {
    // Platforms
    wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
    android: { target_os = "android" },
    macos: { target_os = "macos" },
    linux: { target_os = "linux" },
    // Backends
    surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
    glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
    wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
    dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
}
```
After you put this in your build script you can then check for those conditions like so:

```
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```

# cfg_aliases - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg_aliases/latest/cfg_aliases/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cfg-aliases)CFG Aliases

CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro that doesn’t have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in

`syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.You use the the [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro in your

`build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[build-dependencies]
cfg_aliases = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**

```
use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
fn main() {
    // Setup cfg aliases
    cfg_aliases! {
        // Platforms
        wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
        android: { target_os = "android" },
        macos: { target_os = "macos" },
        linux: { target_os = "linux" },
        // Backends
        surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
        glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
        wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
        dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
    }
}
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:

```
#[cfg(wasm)]
println!("This is running in WASM");
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
println!("We're running in WASM");
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "22")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!

```
if cfg!(glutin) {
    // use glutin
} else {
    // Do something else
}
#[cfg(all(glutin, surfman))]
compile_error!("You cannot specify both `glutin` and `surfman` features");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#syntax-and-error-messages)Syntax and Error Messages

The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.

Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn’t a real limitation because that doesn’t make logical sense anyway:

[§](https://docs.rs#attribution-and-thanks)Attribution and Thanks

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3)some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2)the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the `tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`[bringing it up](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13)on the Rust forum.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html)- aliases

# cfg_aliases 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cfg_aliases/0.2.0

# CFG Aliases

CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [`cfg_aliases!`] macro that doesn't have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in `syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.

You use the the [`cfg_aliases!`] macro in your `build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.

## Example

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[]
 = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**

```
use cfg_aliases;
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:

```
println!;
println!;
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
println!;
println!;
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!

```
if cfg!  else
compile_error!;
```
## Syntax and Error Messages

The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.

Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn't a real limitation because that doesn't make logical sense anyway:

```
// This causes an error!
cfg_aliases!
```
## Attribution and Thanks

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3)some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2)the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the `tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`[bringing it up](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13)on the Rust forum.

# CFG Aliases
CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [`cfg_aliases!`] macro that doesn't have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in `syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.
You use the the [`cfg_aliases!`] macro in your `build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.
## Example
**Cargo.toml:**
```toml
[build-dependencies]
cfg_aliases = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**
```rust
use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
fn main() {
    // Setup cfg aliases
    cfg_aliases! {
        // Platforms
        wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
        android: { target_os = "android" },
        macos: { target_os = "macos" },
        linux: { target_os = "linux" },
        // Backends
        surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
        glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
        wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
        dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
    }
}
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:
```rust
#[cfg(wasm)]
println!("This is running in WASM");
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:
```rust
#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
println!("We're running in WASM");
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!
```rust
if cfg!(glutin) {
    // use glutin
} else {
    // Do something else
}
#[cfg(all(glutin, surfman))]
compile_error!("You cannot specify both `glutin` and `surfman` features");
```
## Syntax and Error Messages
The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.
Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn't a real limitation because that doesn't make logical sense anyway:
```rust,ignore
// This causes an error!
cfg_aliases! {
    test1: { not(test2) },
    test2: { not(test1) },
}
```

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me][sm] some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out][po] the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the [`tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`] macro from which most of the cfg attribute parsing logic is taken from. Also thanks to @ratmice for [bringing it up][bip] on the Rust forum.
[`tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`]: https://docs.rs/tectonic_cfg_support/0.0.1/src/tectonic_cfg_support/lib.rs.html#166-298
[po]: https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2
[bip]: https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13
[sm]: https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3
```

[174](https://docs.rs#174)#[macro_export]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)macro_rules! cfg_aliases {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    // Helper that just checks whether the CFG environment variable is set
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    (@cfg_is_set $cfgname:ident) => {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            let cfg_var = stringify!($cfgname).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_");
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            let result = std::env::var(format!("CARGO_CFG_{}", &cfg_var)).is_ok();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            // CARGO_CFG_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS _should_ be set for when debug assertions are enabled,
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            // but as of writing is not: see https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/5777
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            if !result && cfg_var == "DEBUG_ASSERTIONS" {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)                std::env::var("PROFILE") == Ok("debug".to_owned())
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            } else {
[187](https://docs.rs#187)                result
[188](https://docs.rs#188)            }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    };
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    // Helper to check for the presense of a feature
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    (@cfg_has_feature $feature:expr) => {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            std::env::var(
[195](https://docs.rs#195)                format!(
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                    "CARGO_FEATURE_{}",
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                    &stringify!($feature).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_").replace('"', "")
[198](https://docs.rs#198)                )
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            ).map(|x| x == "1").unwrap_or(false)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    };
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    // Helper that checks whether a CFG environment contains the given value
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    (@cfg_contains $cfgname:ident = $cfgvalue:expr) => {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        std::env::var(
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            format!(
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                "CARGO_CFG_{}",
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                &stringify!($cfgname).to_uppercase().replace("-", "_")
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            )
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        ).unwrap_or("".to_owned()).split(",").find(|x| x == &$cfgvalue).is_some()
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    };
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    // Emitting `any(clause1,clause2,...)`: convert to `$crate::cfg_aliases!(clause1) && $crate::cfg_aliases!(clause2) && ...`
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    (
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        @parser_emit
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        all
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    ) => {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        ($(
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            ($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($grouped)+))
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        )&&+)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    };
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    // Likewise for `all(clause1,clause2,...)`.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    (
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        @parser_emit
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        any
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ) => {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        ($(
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            ($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($grouped)+))
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        )||+)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    };
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // "@clause" rules are used to parse the comma-separated lists. They munch
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    // their inputs token-by-token and finally invoke an "@emit" rule when the
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    // list is all grouped. The general pattern for recording the parser state
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    // is:
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    //
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    // ```
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    // $crate::cfg_aliases!(
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    //    @clause $operation
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    //    [{grouped-clause-1} {grouped-clause-2...}]
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    //    [not-yet-parsed-tokens...]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    //    current-clause-tokens...
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    // )
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    // ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    // This rule must come first in this section. It fires when the next token
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    // to parse is a comma. When this happens, we take the tokens in the
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    // current clause and add them to the list of grouped clauses, adding
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    // delimeters so that the grouping can be easily extracted again in the
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    // emission stage.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    (
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        @parser_clause
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        $op:ident
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        [, $($rest:tt)*]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        $($current:tt)+
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ) => {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause $op [
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            $(
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                {$($grouped)+}
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            )*
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            {$($current)+}
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        ] [
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            $($rest)*
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        ]);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    };
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    // This rule comes next. It fires when the next un-parsed token is *not* a
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    // comma. In this case, we add that token to the list of tokens in the
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    // current clause, then move on to the next one.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    (
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        @parser_clause
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        $op:ident
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        [$tok:tt $($rest:tt)*]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        $($current:tt)*
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ) => {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause $op [
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            $(
[283](https://docs.rs#283)                {$($grouped)+}
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            )*
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        ] [
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            $($rest)*
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        ] $($current)* $tok);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    };
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    // This rule fires when there are no more tokens to parse in this list. We
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    // finish off the "current" token group, then delegate to the emission
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    // rule.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    (
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        @parser_clause
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        $op:ident
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        []
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        $($current:tt)+
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ) => {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_emit $op
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            $(
[302](https://docs.rs#302)                {$($grouped)+}
[303](https://docs.rs#303)            )*
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            {$($current)+}
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        );
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    };
[307](https://docs.rs#307)
[308](https://docs.rs#308)
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    // `all(clause1, clause2...)` : we must parse this comma-separated list and
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    // partner with `@emit all` to output a bunch of && terms.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    (
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        @parser
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        all($($tokens:tt)+)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ) => {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause all [] [$($tokens)+])
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    };
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    // Likewise for `any(clause1, clause2...)`
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    (
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        @parser
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        any($($tokens:tt)+)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    ) => {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser_clause any [] [$($tokens)+])
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    };
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // `not(clause)`: compute the inner clause, then just negate it.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    (
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        @parser
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        not($($tokens:tt)+)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    ) => {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        !($crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($tokens)+))
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    };
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    // `feature = value`: test for a feature.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    (@parser feature = $value:expr) => {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_has_feature $value)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    };
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    // `param = value`: test for equality.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    (@parser $key:ident = $value:expr) => {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_contains $key = $value)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    };
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    // Parse a lone identifier that might be an alias
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    (@parser $e:ident) => {
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        __cfg_aliases_matcher__!($e)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    };
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    // Entrypoint that defines the matcher
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    (
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        @with_dollar[$dol:tt]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        $( $alias:ident : { $($config:tt)* } ),* $(,)?
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    ) => {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        // Create a macro that expands other aliases and outputs any non
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        // alias by checking whether that CFG value is set
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        macro_rules! __cfg_aliases_matcher__ {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            // Parse config expression for the alias
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            $(
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                ( $alias ) => {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                    $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($config)*)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                };
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            )*
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            // Anything that doesn't match evaluate the item
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            ( $dol e:ident ) => {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                $crate::cfg_aliases!(@cfg_is_set $dol e)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)            };
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        $(
[368](https://docs.rs#368)            println!("cargo:rustc-check-cfg=cfg({})", stringify!($alias));
[369](https://docs.rs#369)            if $crate::cfg_aliases!(@parser $($config)*) {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)                println!("cargo:rustc-cfg={}", stringify!($alias));
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            }
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        )*
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    };
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    // Catch all that starts the macro
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    ($($tokens:tt)*) => {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        $crate::cfg_aliases!(@with_dollar[$] $($tokens)*)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    }
[379](https://docs.rs#379)}

# cfg_aliases in cfg_aliases - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cfg_aliases/latest/target-redirect/cfg_aliases/macro.cfg_aliases.html

```
macro_rules! cfg_aliases {
    (@cfg_is_set $cfgname:ident) => { ... };
    (@cfg_has_feature $feature:expr) => { ... };
    (@cfg_contains $cfgname:ident = $cfgvalue:expr) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_emit
        all
        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_emit
        any
        $({$($grouped:tt)+})+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        [, $($rest:tt)*]
        $($current:tt)+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        [$tok:tt $($rest:tt)*]
        $($current:tt)*
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser_clause
        $op:ident
        [$({$($grouped:tt)+})*]
        []
        $($current:tt)+
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        all($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        any($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (
        @parser
        not($($tokens:tt)+)
    ) => { ... };
    (@parser feature = $value:expr) => { ... };
    (@parser $key:ident = $value:expr) => { ... };
    (@parser $e:ident) => { ... };
    (
        @with_dollar[$dol:tt]
        $( $alias:ident : { $($config:tt)* } ),* $(,)?
    ) => { ... };
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Create `cfg` aliases

**build.rs:**

```
// Setup cfg aliases
cfg_aliases! {
    // Platforms
    wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
    android: { target_os = "android" },
    macos: { target_os = "macos" },
    linux: { target_os = "linux" },
    // Backends
    surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
    glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
    wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
    dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
}
```
After you put this in your build script you can then check for those conditions like so:

```
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
